title: Difficult Ethical Choices
keyIdea: An ethical dilemma is a choice where two good values pull different ways, such as honesty and kindness, or loyalty and safety. Name the values first. Then weigh the consequences: who could be helped or harmed, and how badly. Harm that cannot be undone weighs the most, so a secret that hides danger should go to a trusted adult. Give real reasons, not “everyone does it”, and look for a choice that respects both values.

kid: Some choices are easy: do not take your friend's lunch. A dilemma is harder. Every option costs something you care about. Gran knits you a jumper you do not like and asks if you love it. Honesty says tell the truth. Kindness says do not hurt her. Both are good, and they pull different ways.

Start by naming the values. Values are the things people care about: honesty, kindness, loyalty, safety, fairness and courage. When you name the two that clash, you can see why the choice feels hard. It does not mean one side is bad.

Next, weigh the consequences. Ask who could be helped or harmed by each choice, and how badly. Ben makes you promise not to tell that he will cycle to the lake alone after dark. Breaking the promise may make him cross for a while. Keeping it could let him get badly hurt, and that cannot be undone. Safety wins, so tell a trusted adult.

Check your reasons. Good reasons name a value or a person who is helped or harmed. “Everyone does it”, “I won't get caught” and “because I said so” are not reasons something is right. Last, look for a third way. You can thank Gran for her time and say which part you like. That is honest and kind at once.
adult: The PSHE Association plan for Key Stage 2 asks pupils to manage dilemmas and to see that values can clash. It also asks them to know when to break a confidence. A secret that puts someone at risk of harm should go to a trusted adult. CASEL calls this skill responsible decision-making: weighing the effects on self and others, with care for ethics and safety.

A simple routine for nine to eleven year olds has four moves. Name the two values in tension. Weigh the consequences: who is affected, how badly, and can the harm be undone? Test the reasons. Popularity, a rule with no reason, or the chance of being caught do not make a choice right. Then look for a third option that keeps both values, such as honesty said kindly.

Common mistakes: treating every dilemma as good against bad, so one side is written off as wrong. Keeping a promise when the secret hides danger. Counting how many reasons sit on each side, not how serious they are. Accepting that everyone does it. Seeing only the two extremes. Be careful to praise the thinking, not just the answer, since fair people can disagree on close cases.

In the lab your child names the two values in three dilemmas. They put five consequence cards on a balance and watch harm that cannot be undone tip it towards telling. Then they sort real reasons from fake ones and pick the option that respects both values.

familyTip: At dinner, share a small dilemma from your own day, such as a friend asking you to cover for them. Ask your child which two values clash, who could be hurt and how badly, and whether there is a third way. Talk about the reasons rather than judging the answer.

visual.caption: Is it a good reason for a choice? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: It keeps a promise that is safe to keep

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name the two values in a dilemma, weigh consequence cards on a balance, sort real reasons, and find a choice that respects both values.

practice.prompt: Your friend shows you a drawing she is proud of. You think it is not very good. Which two values pull against each other?
practice.hint: One value is about telling the truth. The other is about not hurting her feelings.
practice.explain: Telling the truth is honesty, and not hurting her is kindness. You can do both: say which part you like and give one gentle tip.

practice.prompt: On a balance, the reasons to tell weigh {a} and {b}. The reasons to keep a secret weigh {c}. How much heavier is the tell side?
practice.hint: Add the two weights on the tell side, then take away the keep side.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} on the tell side, and {=a+b} − {c} = {=a+b-c}. The tell side is heavier by {=a+b-c}.

practice.prompt: Which is a real reason to give back money you found?
choices: It belongs to someone who may need it
practice.hint: A real reason names who is helped or harmed, or a value.
practice.explain: The owner may need the money, so returning it is honest and fair. Being seen or copying friends is not a reason it is right.

practice.prompt: A dilemma has {a} possible choices. You rule out {b} because they hurt someone. How many choices are left to weigh?
practice.hint: Start with all the choices and take away the ones you ruled out.

pool.prompt: Why is a dilemma hard to decide?
pool.hint: Think about what each side cares about.
pool.explain: In a dilemma both sides protect a value, so whatever you choose costs something you care about.

pool.prompt: A friend makes you promise not to tell that someone is hurting him. What should you do?
pool.hint: Which matters more here: the promise or his safety?
pool.explain: A secret that hides harm should go to a trusted adult. Safety comes before the promise.

pool.prompt: Which consequence should weigh the most?
choices: Someone may be cross for a day
pool.explain: Being badly hurt may not be undone. Feeling cross or embarrassed passes.

pool.prompt: Which is NOT a real reason that a choice is right?
choices: It is fair to the whole group
pool.hint: Does the reason name a value or who is helped?
pool.explain: “Everyone else is doing it” names no value and no one who is helped, so it is not a real reason.

pool.prompt: You are picking a team. Which choice respects both loyalty and fairness?
choices: Pick by effort and skill, and kindly tell your friend why
Always pick your best friend first
pool.hint: Look for the choice that is fair to everyone and still kind to your friend.
pool.explain: Picking by effort is fair, and explaining kindly keeps the friendship. Both values are respected.

pool.prompt: The tell side of a balance holds weights {a} and {b}. The keep side holds weights 2 and {c}. How heavy is the tell side?
pool.hint: Add only the weights on the tell side.

pool.prompt: {n} children vote on a hard choice. {a} of them vote to tell a teacher. How many vote not to tell?
pool.hint: Take the tell votes away from all the children.

pool.prompt: Which values clash when you see a friend cheat in a test?
pool.hint: One value is about your friend. The other is about the rest of the class.
pool.explain: Sticking by your friend is loyalty, and the class being treated equally is fairness.

pool.prompt: What is a “third way” in a dilemma?
choices: A choice that respects both values
Asking a friend to choose for you
pool.hint: It is a choice that keeps both values in view.
pool.explain: A third way finds a choice that respects both values, like being honest in a kind way.
